title: The Translator Who Invented Korean Christianity
event_summary: In the early 1880s, a Korean merchant named Seo Sang-ryun, working with Scottish missionary John Ross in Mukden, Manchuria, translated the New Testament into Korean — the first complete Korean-language Bible. Seo and fellow Korean collaborator Yi Eung-chan then smuggled copies across the border into Korea, a hermit kingdom that had executed Christians for decades. These translations seeded underground congregations across the Korean peninsula years before any Western missionary ever set foot inside the country.
why_forgotten: Western missionary histories typically credit European and American evangelists for Korea's Christianization, overlooking the Korean laypeople who did the foundational work from foreign soil. Korean nationalist historiography also sometimes downplayed the role of Christian converts, and Seo Sang-ryun died in relative obscurity, overshadowed by the institutional churches that followed.
why_it_matters: South Korea today has one of the largest Christian populations in Asia, with roughly 30% of its citizens identifying as Christian — a demographic force that has profoundly shaped its politics, education system, and global missionary movement. The fact that Korean Christianity was self-planted by Korean translators rather than imposed by colonial missionaries makes it nearly unique among Asian nations and helps explain the religion's extraordinary cultural resilience there.
